outcomes: Fit deterministic k-means to unlabeled feature points and compute summed inertia
Explain Gaussian-mixture responsibilities as normalized component probabilities
Use negative log density as an anomaly score without confusing rarity with harm
lessons: Replace a hard group with a probability
Turn density into an anomaly score

cluster.name: cluster
cluster.definition: A group of unlabeled feature points treated as similar under a chosen representation and distance or density model.
cluster.explanation: Clusters are outputs of modeling choices rather than discovered ground-truth labels. Feature scaling, distance, model family, initialization, and the requested number of groups can all change the partition. A useful cluster should therefore be evaluated against the purpose of the analysis and its stability, not accepted merely because an algorithm returned an integer assignment. External domain evidence can help interpret whether a grouping is actionable.

inertia.name: inertia
inertia.definition: The sum of squared distances from every feature point to its assigned k-means center.
inertia.explanation: K-means alternates assignments and mean updates to reduce inertia. Squared distance makes the arithmetic mean the optimal center for a fixed cluster. This chapter sums one assigned distance for each point; it does not average them. Inertia never increases under exact standard steps, but it typically decreases when k increases and therefore cannot select k by itself. Its scale also changes when feature units or scaling change. Comparing runs requires the same data transformation and distance convention.

gaussian-mixture.name: Gaussian mixture model
gaussian-mixture.definition: A probability density formed by a weighted sum of Gaussian component densities.
gaussian-mixture.explanation: Each component has a mixture weight, mean, and covariance. A feature point can have fractional responsibility for several components, unlike a hard k-means assignment. The reference uses diagonal covariance to avoid matrix inversion and model axis-aligned spreads. Component indices are exchangeable, and likelihood can become singular when a variance collapses, so the implementation floors each variance. The fitted mixture weights remain nonnegative and normalized to one.

responsibility.name: responsibility
responsibility.definition: The posterior probability that one mixture component generated a feature point under current parameters.
responsibility.explanation: Responsibilities normalize component weight times density across all components and sum to one for each point. They are point-specific probabilities, distinct from the model's fitted mixture weights and unnormalized component terms. EM uses them as fractional counts: their component-wise sum determines effective mass, weighted mean, variance, and an updated mixture weight. Stable implementations normalize log terms rather than dividing raw densities that may underflow. Ambiguous points can therefore influence several components at once.

expectation-maximization.name: expectation-maximization
expectation-maximization.definition: An alternating procedure for maximum-likelihood estimation with hidden variables.
expectation-maximization.explanation: For a Gaussian mixture, the E-step calculates posterior component responsibilities. The M-step uses those fractional assignments to update weights, means, and variances. Under the standard unconstrained derivation, observed-data likelihood does not decrease. Practical variance floors and dead-component policies prevent singularities but must be documented because they modify the exact optimization problem. A maximum iteration count prevents an endless numerical convergence loop.

anomaly-score.name: anomaly score
anomaly-score.definition: A numeric ranking of how unusual a feature point is under a fitted reference model.
anomaly-score.explanation: This chapter uses negative log mixture density, so low-density points receive larger scores. A score becomes an alarm only after a threshold is calibrated on separate representative data. Density and thresholds depend on feature units, dimension, and population drift. Statistical rarity does not determine whether a point is harmful, erroneous, or valuable; that judgment requires domain investigation. False-positive and detection rates must accompany any deployed threshold.

sources.title: Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations
Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm
Pattern Clustering by Multivariate Mixture Analysis

checks: K-means finds one negative and one positive fixture center with summed inertia below 3
Final assignments are recomputed from the returned centers
Mixture responsibilities sum to one and component weights remain normalized
The distant point receives a larger anomaly score than a cluster-center point
Later well-conditioned EM fits do not reduce summed fixture log-likelihood beyond tolerance
limitations: Empty k-means centers are retained rather than reseeded
The GMM supports diagonal two-dimensional components only
No anomaly threshold is estimated from the tiny training fixture
